headline: Legendary Strategist Warns of Decade Stretch; Market Ignores Him Anyway
subheadline: David Rosenberg's four-decade career of correct calls apparently irrelevant when AI narrative is this good.
source_headline: Rosenberg warns of most stretched market in his 40-year career
body_html:
David Rosenberg, the market strategist who has spent four decades watching bubbles inflate and pop with the precision of a man who has seen this exact film too many times, recently delivered a warning so blunt it barely qualifies as prediction: we are living in the most stretched market conditions of his entire professional life. This is not a man prone to hyperbole. This is a man who watched the tech bubble of 2000, the housing catastrophe of 2008, and somehow kept his sanity intact. His concern, documented by the Financial Post, centers on two intertwined pathologies: the reliance on artificial intelligence to justify further market appreciation, and the fragilities lurking beneath the surface of the U.S. economy itself.

The particularly delicious irony here is that Rosenberg's warning arrives precisely as the mechanism he identifies—AI as valuation fuel—continues its unopposed march through capital markets. Markets operate under a curious logic: the moment a legitimate structural concern is publicly articulated by someone credible enough to make the financial press, that same concern becomes proof that the system is working, that someone is watching, that everything is monitored. The presence of a warning, in other words, becomes an excuse for inaction. Regulators point to the warning. Investors cite the warning as evidence of informed risk management. Journalists write about the warning. Life continues unchanged.

What makes Rosenberg's particular warning noteworthy is not its novelty—market strategists have been generating warnings since the moment the S&P 500 decided to trade on hope rather than fundamentals—but rather its pedigree and its timing. A four-decade career represents multiple market cycles, multiple corrections, multiple regime changes. It is not the career of someone who cries wolf. It is the career of someone who has earned the right to point at the wolf, describe its exact location, weight, and bite force, and watch people continue walking toward the forest anyway.

The AI narrative has become the market's operating system in 2024 and beyond. Every acquisition gets rebranded as an AI play. Every earnings call pivots to mention machine learning. Every fund prospectus now includes the mandatory paragraph about how their thesis touches artificial intelligence in some adjacent way. This is not due diligence—this is cargo cult investing. The underlying fragilities Rosenberg references—structural weaknesses in the actual U.S. economy that exist independent of sentiment—remain unaddressed and un-priced because they conflict with the story the market has decided to tell itself.

History suggests that the moment a veteran strategist warns of maximum stretch in market conditions, we are usually somewhere in the second or third inning of a process that ends in correction. Not always immediately. Sometimes the stretch extends further than any rational observer predicted. But the pattern is clear: complacency masquerading as risk management, followed by a sudden recalibration. The recognition that fragilities, when ignored long enough, eventually demand attention.

Rosenberg's warning will be cited frequently in the post-correction analysis. Investment committees will nod solemnly while reviewing the Financial Post article. Compliance departments will file it away as evidence of appropriate concern. And in the meantime, the reliance on AI narratives to justify valuations will continue unopposed, because the belief that this time is different remains far more profitable than the belief that Rosenberg might be right.

In markets, being correct is optional. Being profitable is mandatory. Rosenberg chose the wrong metric.
glossary_definition: Structural weaknesses in an economy that are impossible to fix but perfectly easy to ignore until they suddenly matter more than narrative.
